blocks.content: Lakshadweep is administered directly by the Union Government without a Legislative Assembly, and — like DNH&DD — has recently been under the additional-charge administration of a single Administrator shared with another UT. This chapter also covers the significant, actively controversial administrative reforms proposed from 2021 onward.

Lakshadweep is a Union Territory administered by the President of India through an Administrator appointed under Article 239 of the Constitution — it has no Legislative Assembly, placing it in the same structural category as Chandigarh, Ladakh, DNH&DD, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

As of 2026, the Administrator is Shri Praful Khoda Patel, holding the post on additional charge since 5 December 2020, alongside his substantive position as Administrator of the separate UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu — a dual-UT administrative arrangement paralleling Vinai Kumar Saxena's dual Delhi-then-Ladakh LG appointments discussed in the companion volumes for those territories.
The judiciary of Lakshadweep falls under the jurisdiction of the Kerala High Court, reflecting the territory's close historical and administrative ties to the Malabar/Kerala coast (Chapter 2).

blocks.content: From late 2020/early 2021, Administrator Praful Khoda Patel introduced a series of significant proposed administrative and regulatory changes, including the draft Lakshadweep Development Authority Regulation (LDAR) 2021 (which critics argued could enable large-scale land acquisition/redevelopment with reduced local consultation), amendments to the Lakshadweep Panchayat Regulation (reducing the number of children permitted for panchayat candidacy eligibility), a proposed Prevention of Anti-Social Activities Regulation (allowing preventive detention, drawing comparison to laws used in more security-sensitive contexts), and a proposed ban on beef and cattle slaughter — a significant change given the islands' near-entirely Muslim population and traditional dietary practices (Chapter 6).

These proposed changes generated substantial local protest and wider national political controversy, with critics (including several Kerala political leaders, given the islands' close social and administrative ties to Kerala) characterising them as a significant, rapid departure from Lakshadweep's historically light-touch, locally sensitive administrative approach, while supporters characterised them as necessary modernisation and development measures.

Several of the more contested provisions were subsequently modified, delayed, or clarified following the public backlash, and the episode remains a significant, frequently referenced example of administrator-versus-local-population tension in India's smaller, no-Assembly Union Territories — a useful comparative case alongside similar governance-friction themes covered in the companion Delhi and J&K GS volumes (albeit in those cases involving an elected government rather than purely local civil-society opposition).

★ EXAM POINT: The 2021 Lakshadweep Development Authority Regulation (LDAR) controversy is a frequently tested current-affairs-cum-polity episode — remember its core contested elements: land-development powers, panchayat-candidacy child-limit rules, preventive-detention provisions, and the beef-ban proposal, and that it generated significant public protest before being partially modified.
